read.sections.0.heading.source: A letter writer in colonial Java
read.sections.0.heading.back: A letter writer in colonial-era Java

read.sections.0.text.source: Raden Ajeng Kartini was born in 1879 in Jepara, on the island of Java. At that time, the Netherlands ruled Java as a colony. Her father was a local leader, and she went to school until she was about 12. That was more schooling than most girls in Java had. Then, like other girls from noble families, she had to stay at home until she married. She kept reading, and she wrote many letters, mostly in Dutch, to friends. She wrote about why girls should be able to learn and choose their own path. A letter shows one person's hopes. It cannot speak for every girl in Java. Today her letters are kept in archives in the Netherlands and Indonesia.
read.sections.0.text.back: Raden Ajeng Kartini was born in 1879 in Jepara, on the island of Java. At that time, the Netherlands ruled Java as a colony. Her father was a local leader, and she went to school until she was about 12 years old. That was longer than the schooling of most girls in Java. Then, like other girls from noble families, she had to stay at home until she married. She kept reading, and she wrote many letters, mostly in Dutch, to her friends. She wrote about why girls should be able to learn and choose their own path in life. A letter shows the hopes of one human being. The letter cannot speak for every girl in Java. Today, her letters are kept in archives in the Netherlands and Indonesia.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Kartini was born in 1879 on the island of Java. The Netherlands ruled Java then. Her father was a local leader. She went to school until she was about 12. Then she had to stay at home. She wrote many letters to friends. She wrote that girls should be able to learn. A letter shows what one person hoped. It does not speak for every girl. Today her letters are kept in an archive.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Kartini was born in 1879 on the island of Java. The Netherlands ruled Java at that time. Her father was a local leader. She went to school until she was about 12 years old. Then she had to stay at home. She wrote many letters to her friends. She wrote that girls should be able to learn. A letter shows the hopes of one human being. The letter does not speak for every girl. Today, her letters are kept in an archive.

read.sections.1.text.source: In October 1901, Kartini wrote a long letter to a friend. She wrote that she and her sisters hoped to open a school one day. It would teach more than books: handwork, cooking, wood-carving and painting too. In the same letter, she wrote about a different plan. The colonial government was planning schools for girls, and Kartini had been asked to teach in one. These were two plans, not one. We can read her letter in an English translation from 1921. Years after her death, an editor chose which letters to print, and the English book kept only some of them.
read.sections.1.text.back: In October 1901, Kartini wrote a long letter to a friend. She wrote that she and her sisters hoped to open a school one day. The school would teach more than books: handwork, cooking, wood-carving and painting too. In the same letter, she wrote about another plan. The colonial government was planning schools for girls, and Kartini had been asked to teach in one of those schools. These were two plans, not one. We can read her letter in an English translation from 1921. Years after her death, an editor chose which letters to print, and the English book only kept some of them.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: In 1901, Kartini wrote a long letter. She and her sisters hoped to open a school. It would teach books, and also cooking and art. In the same letter, she wrote about another plan. The government planned schools for girls. It asked Kartini to teach. These were two different plans. We read the letter in an English translation from 1921. An editor chose which letters to print. So we do not have all her words.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: In 1901, Kartini wrote a long letter. She and her sisters hoped to open a school. The school would teach books, and also cooking and art. In the same letter, she wrote about another plan. The government planned schools for girls. The government asked Kartini to teach. These were two different plans. We read the letter in an English translation from 1921. An editor chose which letters to print. So we do not have all her words.

read.sections.2.text.source: On 7 July 1903, the colonial government made a decision. It offered Kartini and her sister Roekmini a scholarship, money to study in Batavia, the city now called Jakarta. A record of this decision is kept in Indonesia's national archive. A decision shows what officials agreed to at one moment. It does not prove that anyone used the money. In fact, the sisters did not use it, and later that year Kartini married. The second picture is her portrait, printed in a book in 1922, long after her death. It shows her face, not her thoughts.
read.sections.2.text.back: On 7 July 1903, the colonial government made a decision. The government offered Kartini and her younger sister Roekmini a scholarship, namely money to study in Batavia, the city now called Jakarta. A record of this decision is kept in Indonesia's national archive. A decision shows what officials agreed to at one moment. The decision does not prove that anyone used the money. In fact, the sisters did not use it, and later that year Kartini married. The second picture is her portrait, printed in a book in 1922, long after her death. The portrait shows her face, not her thoughts.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: On 7 July 1903, the government made a decision. It gave Kartini and her sister a scholarship. This was money to study in Batavia, now called Jakarta. An archive in Indonesia keeps the decision. A decision shows what leaders agreed. It does not show what happened next. The sisters did not use the money. The second picture is a portrait of Kartini. It was printed in 1922. It shows her face, not her thoughts.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: On 7 July 1903, the government made a decision. The government gave Kartini and her younger sister a scholarship. This was money to study in Batavia, which is now called Jakarta. An archive in Indonesia keeps the decision. A decision shows what leaders agreed to. The decision does not show what happened after that. The sisters did not use the money. The second picture is a portrait of Kartini. The portrait was printed in 1922. The portrait shows her face, not her thoughts.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Kartini's life touches on things that can be personal: girls kept at home, arranged marriage (her husband already had other wives), and her death a few days after giving birth. The lesson says only that she married in 1903; if the rest comes up, keep it brief and factual. Many learners have had their own schooling interrupted: keep the lesson on Kartini's sources, and never ask learners whether they or girls they know were kept out of school or married young, or about their own or their family's schooling, journeys, country, religion or ethnicity.

Evidence move (brief 3B): keep the sisters' 1901 school hope separate from the government's plan for girls' schools (in the same letter) and from the 1903 decision. A sound answer keeps the letter's aim, the official decision and the outcome distinct. Misconceptions to catch: merging the sisters' school plan with the government plan; thinking the decision proves she studied; treating one noble woman's letters as the voice of all girls in Java. educatorNotes.1.source: Source caveats: the 1921 English edition is a selection of about two-thirds of the 1911 Dutch book, which J.H. Abendanon edited; it carries colonial-era framing from the translator and a foreword, and the Dutch editor notes that some letters from mid-1903 were “not suitable for publication”. Separate Kartini's words from the editors'. Joost Coté's Kartini: The Complete Writings 1898–1904 (2014) is a fuller modern translation. The decision's details (7 July 1903, 4,800 guilders, study in Batavia for Kartini and Roekmini, not used) come from that Dutch edition; the National Archives of Indonesia's catalogue record of it could not be opened from here.
